front.title: Inflation vocabulary
head: Term
Meaning / quick example
rows: Rise in the general price level over time.
Dollars in the year they are received.
Purchasing power expressed in a chosen base year.
Price index for a specified consumer basket; personal costs may differ.

front.title: Future price
front.text: ⟨F=C(1+f)^t⟩. C = today’s price dollars; f = annual decimal inflation; t = years.

front.title: Bring dollars back to today
front.html:
⟨C=\dfrac{F}{(1+f)^t}⟩
F = future dollars; f = annual decimal inflation; t = years; C = today’s purchasing power.
$50,000 received in 20 years at 2.5% inflation:
⟨\dfrac{50{,}000}{1.025^{20}}\approx30{,}513.55⟩
About $30,513.55 today
Use the same base year when comparing amounts.

front.title: CPI & real return
front.html:
⟨\text{Inflation}=\dfrac{\text{CPI}_{2}-\text{CPI}_{1}}{\text{CPI}_{1}}⟩
CPI 200 → 210 gives ⟨\tfrac{10}{200}=5\%⟩.
⟨\text{Real return}=\dfrac{1+r}{1+f}-1⟩
r = nominal return, f = inflation; both decimal rates for the same period.
6% return, 2.5% inflation:
⟨\tfrac{1.06}{1.025}-1\approx3.41\%⟩ real.
Subtracting inflation is a rough approximation.

head: Account

Extra compensation; terms and tax treatment vary.
How much employer money you keep when leaving.

back.title: Project regular saving
back.html:
⟨F=D\dfrac{(1+i)^N-1}{i}⟩
D = end-of-month deposit dollars; i = monthly decimal return; N = months; F = future dollars.
$375 monthly for 42 years at hypothetical 6% nominal, compounded monthly:
⟨i=\tfrac{0.06}{12},\quad N=504⟩
About $851,310.08 future dollars
No starting balance, fees or tax; constant return and deposits.

back.title: Interpret that projection
back.text: Use the same $851,310.08 future balance and 42-year horizon; assume 2.5% annual inflation.
back.example: What purchasing power does it represent?

back.title: Roth or traditional?
back.text: Same $1,000 pretax earnings; both investments double. Eligible traditional deduction; 20% tax now, 10% on later withdrawal.

back.title: When could Roth win?
back.html:
If the later tax rate were 30% instead, with all other assumptions unchanged:
Traditional: ⟨1{,}000(2)(0.70)=1{,}400⟩
Roth: ⟨1{,}000(0.80)(2)=1{,}600⟩
Roth gives $200 more
Equal tax rates give equal after-tax results in this model. Actual choice also depends on eligibility, cash flow, flexibility and uncertain future rates.

back.title: Spending target: a scenario
back.html:
⟨\text{Savings target}=\dfrac{\text{annual spending gap}}{w}⟩
Gap = spending minus other reliable income; w = assumed starting withdrawal fraction.
$40,000 spending − $16,000 other income = $24,000 gap.
At assumed 4%: ⟨\tfrac{24{,}000}{0.04}=600{,}000⟩.
A 4% scenario is not a guarantee. Include taxes, time horizon, fees and market risk; use consistent year dollars.
